label: The Monothelite–Dyothelite Controversy (7th c.)
description: The seventh-century Christological controversy over whether Christ has one will (μονοθελητισμός) or two wills (dyothelitism). Initiated as an imperial unionist policy under Heraclius (Sergius I of Constantinople's Psephos, 633; Ekthesis, 638) and continued under Constans II (Typos, 648), it began with monenergism (one operation/ἐνέργεια) and shifted to monotheletism (one will). Maximus the Confessor, building on Sophronius of Jerusalem, became the principal defender of two natural wills, grounding will (θέλησις) in nature rather than hypostasis and distinguishing the natural will (θέλημα φυσικόν) from the gnomic/deliberative will (γνώμη). The controversy reached its dramatic climax in Maximus' public Disputatio cum Pyrrho (Carthage, July 645), and the dyothelite position prevailed at the Lateran Council (649) and was dogmatically defined at the Third Council of Constantinople (Constantinople III, 680–681), which condemned the monothelites (incl. Patriarchs Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul II, and Pope Honorius I). For the history of the philosophical concept of will, this is a key episode often described (Frede 2011; Dihle 1982; Blowers 2016) as where the natural-vs-gnomic-will distinction is forged.

label: Pope Honorius I (d. 638)
description: Bishop of Rome (625–638). In his correspondence with Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople (Ep. ad Sergium) he assented to the formula of 'one will' in Christ (unum velle), and was posthumously condemned as a monothelite by the Third Council of Constantinople (Constantinople III, 680–681) and in subsequent papal/conciliar acts. A pivotal and contested figure in the monothelite–dyothelite controversy and in later debates over papal authority. Currently MISSING as a KG node (appears only in metadata/descriptions).
evidence: Blowers 2016, Maximus the Confessor (OECS), ch.2 (Sergius' Ep. 1 ad Honorium; n.93 cites Sergius, Ep. 1 ad Honorium in Allen, Sophronius of Jerusalem, 188–191); standard church history. Honorius condemned at Constantinople III (681).

rationale: Honorius assented to 'one will' in his reply to Sergius and was condemned as a monothelite at Constantinople III.
Posthumously condemned as a monothelite (Constantinople III); his 'unum velle' aligned him with the monothelite party. Weight <1 because his role is debated and partly a matter of imprecise wording.
